questions.question_stem: A suspect holds 50,000 USDT, issued by Tether, and 20 ETH on a rollup. Who could stop each holding?
questions.correct_answer: Tether could freeze the USDT; no issuer stands behind ETH; the sequencer could only delay either one's next transaction.
incorrect_answers: Tether could freeze the USDT, and the sequencer could stop the ETH for good, because it alone orders every transaction.
Nobody could stop either holding, because an issuer's freeze reaches only Ethereum and a sequencer only orders transactions.
Tether could freeze the USDT, and Ethereum's validators could freeze the ETH, because they record every batch the rollup posts.
questions.explanation: An issuer can freeze its own token, and nobody issues ETH. The sequencer orders every transaction, so it can delay the next one, but the user can force it through Ethereum after a wait. Saying the sequencer can stop funds names the right party but the wrong power.

questions.question_stem: A suspect starts moving 30 ETH out of an optimistic rollup. Twelve minutes later, 29.9 ETH reaches the suspect's address on Ethereum. What does the timing suggest?
questions.correct_answer: Not the native bridge, which waits about a week; someone else paid on Ethereum, as a liquidity or intents bridge does.
incorrect_answers: The native bridge, because a withdrawal finishes once the sequencer posts the batch, and the shortfall was the bridge's fee.
The native bridge, because the challenge period applies only to deposits, so a withdrawal clears as soon as it is posted.
A forged message, because only a message bridge can finish an exit faster than the rollup's challenge period allows.
questions.explanation: An optimistic rollup's own bridge makes withdrawals wait out the challenge period. A payout in minutes means another party paid from its own funds on Ethereum, which is what liquidity and intents bridges do. The slightly lower amount fits a fee.

questions.question_stem: On Ethereum, an address sends 10,000 USDC to a bridge's deposit contract, and the deposit's event names Arbitrum and that address as recipient. On Arbitrum, 9,990 USDC arrives from an ordinary address whose own balance falls by 9,990. No tokens are created. Which type and confidence fit?
questions.correct_answer: Intents, filled by a relayer: High, because the deposit's event names the recipient that was paid.
incorrect_answers: Lock-and-mint: High, because the amounts agree and the 10 USDC gap is the bridge's fee for the copy.
Message-verified: High, because the bridge acted on Arbitrum after a message about the deposit on Ethereum.
Intents, filled by a relayer: Low, because only the amount and the timing link the two records together.
questions.explanation: The far-side question is where chain B's tokens came from. Nothing was created and an ordinary address paid from its own balance, so someone else's funds paid: liquidity or intents. The deposit's event names the paid recipient, so the link is High, not a lead.

questions.question_stem: On Ethereum, 300 ETH goes to THORChain with a memo naming BTC and a Bitcoin address. On Bitcoin, THORChain pays BTC to that address with an OUT: memo naming the deposit's hash. Name the type, who could freeze it, and how sure you are.
questions.correct_answer: Liquidity swap; no issuer, since none issues ETH or BTC; High, because the two memos join the records.
incorrect_answers: Lock-and-mint; no issuer, since none issues ETH or BTC; High, because a lock on Ethereum matches a Bitcoin mint.
Liquidity swap; no issuer, since none issues ETH or BTC; Low, because the ETH amount differs from the BTC paid.
Liquidity swap; the BTC's issuer could freeze it on Bitcoin; High, because the two memos join the records.
questions.explanation: THORChain swaps native coins by having another party pay on the far chain. No issuer stands behind ETH or BTC, so no issuer could freeze it. The deposit's memo names the coin and address and the payout's OUT: memo names the deposit, so the link is High.

questions.question_stem: Only a small share of the money stolen from Bitget was frozen. What best explains this?
questions.correct_answer: Issuers can freeze only their own stablecoins, and most of the money crossed as ETH and other coins with no issuer.
incorrect_answers: Freezes apply only on the chain where the theft began, and the money had already left that chain by the time issuers acted.
Most of the money was wrapped on arrival, and a wrapped token can be frozen only by the bridge that wrapped it.
Privacy tools hid the funds from the issuers, so no issuer could tell which addresses held the stolen stablecoins.
questions.explanation: The type named who could freeze, and for most of Bitget's money no issuer could: ETH and other native coins have none, and Tether and Circle reach only their own stablecoins. The bridges moved the money faster than freezes could land.
questions.lesson_block: Answers: bridges moved it faster than freezes

specific_source.reading: Lesson slide: Answers: bridges moved it faster than freezes

questions.question_stem: An analyst sees wrapped Monero on Ethereum and assumes it is hidden, as Monero is on its own chain. What is the correct reading?
questions.correct_answer: A wrapped token is an ordinary Ethereum token on a public ledger, as visible as any other Ethereum token.
incorrect_answers: Wrapping keeps Monero's privacy, because the bridge that locked the coin also keeps the copy's holders private.
It is visible only while the original coin stays locked, and a burned copy's earlier transfers cannot be read.
It is visible, but only to the bridge's operators, who alone can read the balances of the minted copies.
questions.explanation: Wrapping does not hide a coin. The wrapped copy is created on a public ledger, so every transfer of it can be read like any other Ethereum token, even though the original Monero hides amounts on its own chain.

questions.question_stem: In an intents bridge, a user deposits on chain A and is paid on chain B. Where does the payment on chain B come from?
questions.correct_answer: The relayer's own tokens: nothing is minted, and the relayer is repaid later through Ethereum.
incorrect_answers: A copy that the bridge mints on chain B once the deposit lands; the relayer only passes the message.
The user's own deposit, which the bridge carries across to chain B after the relayer confirms it.
The MEV-Boost relay, which fronts the payment and is repaid by the validators later on.
questions.explanation: In an intent, a relayer pays the user on chain B from its own tokens and is repaid later. Nothing crosses and nothing is minted, which separates it from lock-and-mint. This relayer is not the MEV-Boost relay or a gas relayer.
questions.lesson_block: Intents: you name the result, a relayer pays it

questions.question_stem: A 10 ETH deposit to THORChain is followed 40 minutes later by a 0.27 BTC payout. No memo can be read. What do you write?
questions.correct_answer: Low: only amount and time match, and across a swap the two amounts compare only through a price.
incorrect_answers: High: the payout came 40 minutes after the deposit, and the amounts agree at the exchange rate.
Moderate: the published methods use amount and time, and a payout this close meets their test.
High: both sides are on public chains, so a payout that follows a deposit this closely can be tied to it.
questions.explanation: Published methods that pair a deposit with its arrival by amount and time assume the same coin on both sides, which a swap breaks. Without the memos, amount and time are a lead, so the word is Low. With both memos readable it would be High.
questions.lesson_block: In a swap, only memos tie deposit to payout

questions.question_stem: A proposal says Ethereum should raise its block size so one chain can carry all traffic. Why does the lesson say Ethereum instead keeps L1 small?
questions.correct_answer: Bigger blocks need bigger hardware to check, pushing validation toward data centres and costing decentralization.
incorrect_answers: Bigger blocks make every transaction cost more in gas, so users would move to other chains that keep smaller blocks.
Bigger blocks let a few large validators outvote the rest, so the chain would lose its security guarantee outright.
Bigger blocks cannot hold the batches a rollup posts, so rollups would stop working until blocks were made smaller again.
questions.explanation: If every node checks every transaction, throughput is capped by what an ordinary node can check. Raising it needs bigger hardware, which pushes validation to data centres. So Ethereum keeps L1 small and moves execution to Layer 2s.
questions.lesson_block: Ethereum stays small so anyone can check it

specific_source.reading: Lesson slide: Ethereum stays small so anyone can check it

questions.question_stem: How does Ethereum come to accept an optimistic rollup's batch compared with a ZK rollup's, and what does that do to a withdrawal?
questions.correct_answer: Optimistic: assumed valid unless a fraud proof wins, so a withdrawal waits; ZK: a validity proof is checked, so none waits.
incorrect_answers: Optimistic: a validity proof comes first, so a withdrawal is instant; ZK: assumed valid until challenged, so it waits a week.
Both are assumed valid until someone challenges, so both kinds of withdrawal must wait out the very same challenge window.
Both are checked by a validity proof, but only the optimistic rollup uses a single sequencer, and that adds the wait.
questions.explanation: An optimistic rollup is assumed valid, and during a challenge window anyone may send a fraud proof, so a withdrawal waits about a week. A ZK rollup sends a validity proof with each batch, so a withdrawal needs no delay once it is accepted.
questions.lesson_block: Optimistic waits a week; ZK waits for a proof

specific_source.reading: Lesson slide: Optimistic waits a week; ZK waits for a proof

questions.question_stem: A rollup is rated Stage 1 and has a Security Council. What does the 75% figure say about the council's power?
questions.correct_answer: It is a limit on the council: a message to Ethereum can be blocked or forged only if at least 75% of it is compromised.
incorrect_answers: It is the council's power: any 75% of its members may freeze funds or upgrade the rollup whenever they choose.
It is the share of the rollup's transactions that code now checks, so a quarter of them still depend on a few named people.
It is the approval the council needs for each withdrawal, so no user can leave unless most of its signers agree.
questions.explanation: A Security Council is a named emergency group. At Stage 1 the 75% figure limits it: fewer than 75% of its members cannot block or forge a message. A lower stage means more human power to upgrade, censor or freeze.

questions.question_stem: On chain B, a bridge's contract released a large amount of a token after a message arrived. Chain A shows no event matching the message. What does this suggest, and where does the analyst look?
questions.correct_answer: The message may be forged; the claimed source chain should hold the event the message says happened.
incorrect_answers: It is an ordinary lock-and-mint, because a release needs no source-chain event once the pool is funded.
It is a relayer's fill, because a relayer pays from its own balance and the source chain records nothing yet.
It is a liquidity swap, because a swap's two sides are joined by memos and need not match a source event.
questions.explanation: A message-verified bridge acts when its verifiers accept a message about the other chain. A release with no matching source event is the sign of a forged message, so the analyst checks the claimed source chain, as at Kelp DAO.
questions.lesson_block: Message bridges trust a message: Kelp DAO

questions.question_stem: A rollup's sequencer leaves a user's transaction out of its batches. What can the user do, and what does that show about the sequencer's power?
questions.correct_answer: After a wait, submit it directly to the rollup's contract on Ethereum; the sequencer can delay a transaction but not stop it.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because only the sequencer may submit transactions to the rollup, so it can stop the transaction for good.
Resubmit it through another sequencer on the same rollup, since each rollup runs several competing operators at once.
Ask Ethereum's validators to include it in their next block, since they order every rollup's transactions as well.
questions.explanation: One operator can delay a transaction by leaving it out, but after a wait the user can submit it directly to the rollup's contract on Ethereum. So the answer to who can stop this is delay, not stop.
questions.lesson_block: One sequencer orders each rollup's trades

specific_source.reading: ethereum.org, Optimistic Rollups: the sequencer and forced inclusion through the rollup's contract

questions.question_stem: A user deposits ETH from Ethereum to a rollup. Which records does the analyst find, and what joins them?
questions.correct_answer: A transaction on Ethereum to the rollup's bridge contract, which holds the assets, and a mint of the same amount on the rollup.
incorrect_answers: A transaction on the rollup only, since the assets move onto the rollup and Ethereum keeps nothing but a later batch of them.
A transaction on Ethereum that burns the assets and a mint of the same amount on the rollup, joined by its challenge period.
A transaction on Ethereum and a matching transfer on the rollup, joined by the sequencer that orders both, not a contract.
questions.explanation: A deposit is an Ethereum transaction to the rollup's bridge contract, which holds the assets, and the rollup mints the same amount to the user. Two chains, two records, joined by the bridge contract, the amount and the address.
questions.lesson_block: A deposit and a withdrawal touch both chains

specific_source.reading: ethereum.org, Optimistic Rollups: asset movement, deposits and withdrawals

questions.question_stem: A trainee says a bridge carries the coin from chain A to chain B. What correction does the lesson give?
questions.correct_answer: A coin exists only on its own chain's ledger, so a bridge mints a copy, trusts a message, or has someone else pay.
incorrect_answers: The coin does cross, but only after a challenge period, which is why every bridge withdrawal takes about a week.
The coin crosses inside a batch posted to Ethereum, which is why every bridge leaves a record on Ethereum.
The coin is split in pieces that each chain holds, so neither chain's ledger shows the whole amount at once.
questions.explanation: A coin exists only on its own chain's ledger, so a bridge cannot carry it. It moves a claim: a copy is minted, a message is trusted, or another party pays on the far chain. Each way leaves different evidence and a different possible freezer.
questions.lesson_block: A bridge moves a claim, not the coin

specific_source.reading: ethereum.org, Bridges: how bridges work and the ways value moves between chains

questions.question_stem: A report says stolen funds crossed three bridges within hours, so three bridges were hacked. Which correction fits the Bitget case?
questions.correct_answer: The hack was at the exchange, where forged withdrawal commands reached its wallet servers; bridges were only the route out.
incorrect_answers: At least one bridge was hacked, because funds can leave an exchange's wallets only through a bridge's locked pool.
The bridges were hacked indirectly, because the exchange's keys were stored in each bridge's contract on both chains.
The exchange's cold wallets were hacked, and the bridges then held the stolen coins until the thief claimed them.
questions.explanation: Crossing bridges does not mean a bridge was hacked. At Bitget, attackers injected forged withdrawal commands on the exchange's wallet servers. The bridges, and other swap services, only carried the money out.
questions.lesson_block: Bitget: the hack was at the exchange

specific_source.reading: Bitget security incident account and Bitquery's Bitget investigation: the compromise was at the exchange
